I took a $40K hit in the last big market downturn, and now I’ve got about $250K invested. I want to keep investing through the ups and downs, but how do you figure out which quality stocks are worth holding during periods like this?
A professional set up my portfolio around quality stocks and broad market ETFs. I'm up around 80% since February, and having a solid plan has made a huge difference in how I handle market volatility.
@Ardra-l8v Nice work. Who are you getting ideas from?
Name’s Elizabeth Joan Vella. Heard her speak at a conference a while back, she’s fairly well known.

The problem with protecting a portfolio against major market crashes is that the defensive allocation needs to be quite substantial to make a meaningful difference, inevitably coming at the expense of long-term returns. A 20% defensive allocation offers relatively limited protection, whereas something in the region of 40–50% starts to have a significant impact on growth. There really is no free lunch: meaningful downside protection comes at a considerable opportunity cost. Instead, I just keep a buffer in cash / money market funds / premium bonds that I hope will be sufficient to buy me enough time to avoid having to withdraw from equities during a crash.
Me too.

Rather than percentage of portfolio, I would think in terms of number of years your cash / money market fund reserves will last before you're forced to sell investments. For someone with a large portfolio, 1% might last 5 years. Someone with a smaller portfolio might need 50% to last the same 5 years.

Everyone's trying to make money on inference, and I don't believe that's a viable business model long term because open-source, open-weight models can just distil from those expensive frontier models and get 90% of the way there with way less capex.

And that sucks for those companies, but it kind of shows that there's not much benefit in serving these frontier models at inference.

So what I think is going to happen is that the only way these businesses can make money is if the frontier labs stop serving inference for their frontier models.

Instead, they train extremely good models internally and use them to solve world-changing problems.

We're already starting to see this with some of the maths findings. But what happens if they start curing cancer?

Say OpenAI internally discovers a drug that can cure a particular type of cancer. Well, they could then go to AstraZeneca or someone and say, "Hey, we have this. We know it works. We want to sell it to you for $50 billion."

They don't necessarily have to manufacture it themselves, although maybe they could if they had the expertise.

Then they just do the next one, and the next one, and the next one. Suddenly, they have a very viable business model where they're solving extremely valuable problems rather than serving out the models.

They can sell those solutions or execute on them themselves through spin-off businesses, and make a ton of money.

That's how I think things will play out, and it's the only viable business model I can really see going forward. I actually think it's quite a viable one.

So my current view is that I don't think a collapse is inevitable, because there is a viable business model here that I don't think many people are talking about.
